name: Sleeping position for face symmetry

lead: The belief is that sleeping on one side presses and distorts the face over years, so sleeping on the back protects symmetry.
No study has tested this. General references on symmetry list development, aging and prenatal factors as causes of asymmetry, and sleep position only appears as one contributor to wrinkles.

paras: The proposed mechanism is prolonged mechanical pressure on one side of the face during sleep. This has not been measured in published research.
Sleep-position reviews note that back sleeping can worsen positional sleep apnea and snoring in some people. No documented harms are specific to this claim.

lead: Sleeping position for face symmetry is a looksmaxxing belief that the posture a person sleeps in affects facial symmetry, with sleeping on the back often described as the way to avoid asymmetry caused by pressing one side of the face into a pillow.

Mainstream sources do not establish that sleep posture determines facial symmetry. A general reference on facial symmetry lists development, aging and prenatal factors among causes of asymmetry and does not mention sleep posture [1]. A general reference on skin wrinkles lists habitual sleeping positions as one of several contributors to wrinkles, without describing the size of the effect [2].

paras: The three main sleeping positions are side (lateral), back (supine) and stomach (prone). Side sleeping is the most common in adults, followed by back sleeping [3]. Sleep-position research mostly concerns health outcomes such as infant sleep safety, positional sleep apnea and reflux rather than facial shape [3].

Facial asymmetry has several documented origins. A small offset of the face relative to the ears is typical and is larger in newborns, asymmetry becomes more noticeable with age as soft tissue changes, and prenatal alcohol exposure alters asymmetry patterns [1]. Research on attractiveness finds that symmetry increases ratings of attractiveness, more strongly for female faces, while perfectly symmetric faces are rated as less natural [1].

No studies found on sleeping position and facial symmetry in the adult face. Related literature covers sleep position and wrinkles, where dermatology sources list habitual sleep position as a contributing factor [2].

In discussions of mewing, back sleeping is sometimes preferred because tongue posture may be easier to maintain; this is described as anecdotal [4]. Sleep-position reviews report that back sleeping can worsen positional sleep apnea in some people [3].
